dek: A Las Vegas pick seller who says he started in 1968 and who ran National Sports Services, one of the best known phone and TV tout businesses. Today his own store sells 30 days of all sports for $149, and the SportsCapping network lists 24 more packages from $30.00 to $1,999.95. The network guarantee pays in free time, not cash. Every record we saw is chosen or graded by the selling side.

short_answer: Jim Feist is a real and very old name in the pick selling business. His own site gives a Las Vegas mailing address and phone number and sells a 30 day all sports package for $149. A 2005 federal court opinion describes him as the President and Chairman of National Sports Services, Inc., which ran Jim Feist Sports, phone lines, magazine ads and jimfeist.com. Today the same name is also sold through the SportsCapping network, which lists 24 packages and grades his picks.

Whether the picks make money is a separate question. The network leaderboard, kept by the side that sells him, shows a strong 2026 WNBA season (62 wins, 39 losses, No. 1 on that board) and a small NFL profit this season (50-42-2, about 2.3% return). He does not appear on the network's all sports boards for all time or this season, which on 20 Nov 2026 listed only cappers who were in profit. Several sales lines did not match the leaderboard on the same day.

Buyer talk is old and mostly about sales methods: free picks leading to calls offering bigger packages. A Connecticut buyer who said he spent more than $100,000 sued in 2003 and lost, because he had signed a release for a $5,000 credit. Former telemarketers alleged in 1999 that several services sold as separate were one operation; that was one side of a lawsuit, not a finding. Treat the name as famous, not proven, and record every pick yourself.

guarantee: SportsCapping, which runs checkout for the network listings, says on its Profit Guarantee page that a guaranteed purchase triggers when its picks "finish with a total profit of zero or less, breaking even counts." A guaranteed package then gets "the handicapper's next day of picks in the same sport, free," and a guaranteed subscription "is automatically extended by its original length." Some accounts get account credit for the amount paid instead.

The fine print says "Season and rest-of-season passes are not guaranteed," replacement picks carry no guarantee of their own, and "Guarantees apply once per purchase." The older Capper Reviews policy page in the same network says plainly that it does not offer a money back policy.

On jimfeist.com the $149 package page states no guarantee. The site terms mention a refund only when the store itself cancels an order ("If we cancel your order, we will notify you and issue a refund") and cap the seller's total liability at what you paid in the last six months.
A buyer who loses money betting the picks gets, at best, more picks. Losses on the bets themselves are never covered, and they are usually far larger than the package price.

claims_note: How we checked: SportsCapping publishes leaderboards by sport and period. We read the underlying data for every sport on 20 Nov 2026. Each board lists only cappers with a positive profit, so a missing name means the capper was not in profit on that board or had too few picks, not that the record is hidden. Profit is in dollars at the network's standard stake, and ROI is profit divided by money risked.
On football the gap is clear: the sales line says up $60 at 5.0% ROI, while the board for the same season says up $237 at 2.3%. Both are small edges. Both come from the selling network.

The WNBA season is the strongest result we found: 62 wins and 39 losses, a 61.4% win rate and a 16.7% return on 101 picks, first on that board. It is one short season, so it says little about the long run.

The experience claims cannot all be true at once. The bio still says "more than 30 years," the product page "over 55 years," and the network copy "60-YEAR." A start in 1968 makes 58 years in 2026. None of these numbers tells you anything about the picks.

The "Yesterday's plays" table on the network pages showed 1 win and 2 losses on 20 Nov 2026 (Colts and Texans over 44 lost, Clippers and Spurs over 225.5 won, Temple minus 2.5 lost), so losing days are shown, which is fair to note.
record: Watchdog graded sample, new 22 Nov 2026. Jim Feist does not publish a complete, time stamped log we can audit, so we built a sample from public posts that carry their plays. Watchdog captures X accounts and forum threads that post or repost picks; the ones naming Jim Feist most often were Churchillsprts, TheGodOfCappers, 1218Sports, EZMSports. From 1 Nov 2026 to 1 Nov 2026 we took every play our parser could read inside a Jim Feist block, kept only those posted before the game started, removed repeats, and graded each one against the final score at one unit risked, at the odds shown or -110 when none were shown.
Result: 3 plays, 2 won, 1 lost, +0.82 units, a return of +27.3% per unit risked. By sport: NFL 2 won, 1 lost, +0.82 units. By month: November 2 won, 1 lost, +0.82 units.
What it means: 3 decided plays is far too few to judge.
What a buyer can verify independently: nothing that we could find. We found no full, time stamped log of every Jim Feist pick with the line, the odds and the release time kept by an outside party.

What the seller side publishes: the network leaderboard by sport and period, streak lines and a yesterday table on the storefronts. These are graded by the same network that sells the picks, on the odds the handicapper selected, so they are the seller's own figures, not an audit. CappersPicks calls its figures documented, and its footer says the storefront is "located in Antigua, West Indies."

jimfeist.com itself shows no record on the pages we read. Its picks area lists categories for Jim's picks and for "Big Mike's Picks," a second capper the site says has worked in the industry since 1986, starting at National Sports Services.

Background: Don Best's handicapper page describes Feist as the head of National Sports Services since the 1970s, with phone lines, websites, Sports Tracker and Proline, and as co author with Kelso Sturgeon of a football betting guide. The 2005 court opinion describes National Sports Services as a Las Vegas company that advertised in national periodicals, ran toll free numbers and jimfeist.com, and sometimes advertised on national TV.

our_data.text: In this edition no Jim Feist pick history is matched to a Watchdog graded record, so we make no claim about how Jim Feist performs beyond what the selling network publishes.
our_data.context: For scale: his best board on the selling network is 61.4% winners in one WNBA season, and his NFL line this season is 54.3%.

customers_intro: Independent customer evidence on Jim Feist is old, spread over four decades, and mostly about the sales process rather than results. The largest pool of current comments sits on a site that is part of the network selling his picks.

customers.text: We found about a dozen independent accounts from 1999 to 2024 across a federal court file, a 1999 Las Vegas Sun report, TheRX (2005), Sportsbook Review (2021 and 2024), a review site (2013 to 2017) and a complaints board. The same themes repeat: a free pick leads to sales calls, then a bigger package, and buyers who lost felt there was no recourse. In a 2005 TheRX thread members described a path from free picks to a $49 weekly package and a $1,000 season, and one said a former call center worker told them staff were told to pick a side. A 2021 SBR member recalls paying $500 for a football weekend in the early 1980s and losing every star rated play, and another described a sales call that followed a free line call. A buyer who said they spent more than $100,000 sued in 2003 and lost because they had signed a release for a $5,000 credit. On the positive side, one 2013 reviewer called the company legitimate after about 10 weeks, and the network's own comment page is mostly favorable. We found no FTC or state regulator action and no independent record showing long run profit.

The Capper Reviews page shows a rating of 3.91 out of 5 from 55 votes and 22 undated comments. Most comments praise his longevity and free picks, a few complain that he is too old or plays too many games in a day. Capper Reviews says it is part of the network that sells these packages, so this is not independent evidence.

A federal court in Connecticut decided a suit by a buyer against National Sports Services, Jim Feist Sports, Jim Feist and a consultant. The opinion says the buyer answered a free pick ad in Pro Football Weekly, was then called by sales staff from September 2000, and bought services worth more than $100,000 in total. After the buyer complained about the picks, the company offered a $5,000 credit in December 2000 in return for a signed statement that they would take no further action. The court held that release barred their claims against the company, found no evidence that Feist had personally dealt with them, and entered judgment for all defendants. The court did not rule on whether the picks were good or bad.

The Las Vegas Sun reported that National Sports Services had sued five former telemarketers for joining a rival. In their answer, the former employees alleged that customers were led to believe they were buying from several unrelated services that all belonged to Jim Feist, that customer details were passed between those services, and that buyers were steered to an offshore sportsbook they said Feist owned. These are one side's allegations in a lawsuit, reported at the time, not court findings, and the company disputed the employees' account.

On TheRX a member asked for experiences because a relative was getting involved with Feist. Replies described free picks leading to a $49 weekly package and then a $1,000 season offer, upselling based on how wealthy a buyer seemed, and a secondhand claim from a former call center worker that staff gave out sides with no real pick behind them. One member said a relative lost thousands. Another called Feist sharp but said the business is mostly hype. Nobody posted a record of following him profitably.

In a Sportsbook Review thread, a member recalled paying $500 for Jim Feist picks on a Las Vegas football weekend around 1982, when they were a student. They said the picks lost 20 stars that weekend without a win and that it nearly ruined them as a beginner.

In the same thread another member said that after calling a free play phone line for a different handicapper, they got a sales call from someone representing Feist offering to sell them winners. A third post in the thread mocked how a lost 1994 Game of the Year was explained on air.
On HandicappingReviews.org a reviewer wrote that the service took $500 and called it "a scam." They gave no details or results, and we could not verify the complaint.
On the same page another reviewer said they had been betting to save for a car and that their losses following the picks ruined that plan. They said they hoped the handicapper would start winning.

On the same page a reviewer said they had tried other popular services and bought these picks for about 10 weeks, and called the company legitimate. They did not say whether they won. The site's own undated review gives mixed feelings and says recent results have not matched his reputation.

On a complaints board, a poster wrote that they were called with promises of large winnings, paid, lost money and could not get it back. They alleged that the company's handicappers release opposite sides of the same games so that someone always wins. No amount, date or reply is shown, and we could not verify it.

In an SBR forum thread where a bettor asked about paid pick services, one member mentioned in passing that Jim Feist was "back," while the replies around it told the poster not to pay any tout. Nobody posted results for Feist.

A Better Business Bureau search for Jim Feist in Las Vegas returned no results and SmartCustomer listed jimfeist.com with zero reviews when we checked on 7 Nov 2026. Our saved archive of the main betting subreddits (824 posts and comments) holds no thread about the service. We found no FTC or state attorney general action naming Feist or National Sports Services.

conflicts: Capper Reviews and CappersPicks, which host the full price list, the star rating and the comments, are part of the SportsCapping network that processes the sale and grades the picks. The leaderboard is kept by the same network.

The Capper Reviews page has carried a banner for a "$1,000 Free Play at MyBookie" linked through an affiliate tracking address. MyBookie is an offshore sportsbook, not licensed by U.S. state regulators. Affiliate deals usually pay the referrer when referred customers sign up or lose.

In 1999 former employees alleged in court papers that buyers were steered to an offshore sportsbook they said Feist owned. That was never proven in anything we read, but it is the kind of interest a buyer should ask about.
jimfeist.com also sells a second capper, Big Mike, under the same store, so the site promotes more than one service.
strengths: A named seller with a Las Vegas mailing address, a phone number and written site terms.
Prices are published for every package on both his store and the network, and the network guarantee rules are written out in detail.
His own store shows one clear and relatively low price: $149 for 30 days of all sports.
The network board shows a strong 2026 WNBA season (No. 1, 62-39) and a small NFL profit this season.
The storefront tables show losing days and a losing "3-6-1" line, not only wins.
The one federal suit we found ended with judgment for the defendants, and we found no regulator action.
concerns: No independent, full record. Every number we saw is chosen or graded by the selling side.
Several sales lines did not match the network's own leaderboard on the same day, and he was absent from the all sports boards that list cappers in profit.
The guarantee gives more picks, never money back, and season passes have no guarantee at all.
The same 30 days costs $149 on his store and $499.95 on the network, and the store title says $199.
Experience claims change from page to page, and contest wins are claimed without being named.
Decades of buyer accounts describe free picks turning into persistent sales calls and bigger packages, and one buyer said he spent more than $100,000.
The reseller page that hosts the rating carries an offshore sportsbook affiliate banner.
checklist: Compare prices first: on 20 Nov 2026 the same 30 days cost $149 on jimfeist.com and $499.95 on the network storefronts.
Open the SportsCapping leaderboard for the sport you want and check whether he appears for This Season and All Time before trusting a streak line.
Ask for every pick from the last 12 months with the line, the odds and the time it was sent. A streak on a sales page is not a record.
Read the guarantee for the words refund, credit and extension. Here every version is free time or credit, and season passes have none.
Expect sales calls if you give a phone number for a free pick, and decide your budget before you answer one.
Never sign a release or a statement about past charges without reading it; in the 2005 case that signature ended the buyer's claims.
Write down each pick yourself the moment you receive it, with the line you can actually get, and give it a few hundred picks before judging.
faq: He is a real, long running seller with a named Las Vegas address, published prices, his own store and a reseller network behind him. We could not verify that his picks win over time, because no independent full record exists. The one federal buyer suit we found ended in judgment for the defendants, and we found no FTC or state regulator action.
What does the Watchdog sample of Jim Feist show?
We graded 3 of their plays that were posted publicly before the game started, 1 Nov 2026 to 1 Nov 2026: 2 won, 1 lost, +0.82 units at one unit each. That is too few plays to judge.
Who is Jim Feist and what was National Sports Services?

His About page says he started in 1968 in Florida, moved to Las Vegas in 1970 and launched the Proline TV show in 1978. A 2005 court opinion describes him as President and Chairman of National Sports Services, Inc., a Las Vegas company that sold handicapping by phone, ads and jimfeist.com, with Jim Feist Sports as one of its divisions.
How much does Jim Feist cost?

On 20 Nov 2026 jimfeist.com sold 30 days of all sports for $149.00. The SportsCapping network storefronts listed single plays at $30.00 and $35.00, one day packages at $39.95, 7 days of all sports at $199.95, one month at $499.95 and 365 days at $1,999.95, with season passes from $125.00 to $899.99.

No cash refunds. Network packages marked guaranteed get free extra time or account credit if they do not profit, season passes carry no guarantee, and the network says it has no money back policy. jimfeist.com states no guarantee and refunds only orders the store itself cancels.
Does Jim Feist have a verified record?

No independent one. The selling network's leaderboard showed him 50-42-2 in the NFL this season and 62-39 in the WNBA season, but he did not appear on its all sports boards for all time or this season, which list only cappers in profit.

You get every play he releases in the period you buy, from one of the oldest names in the business, and on guaranteed packages a free repeat period if you lose. What is unproven is whether his picks beat the roughly 52.4% needed at -110 over hundreds of plays, and nothing refunds the package or your betting losses.
